explanation: A function call convention defines how arguments are passed to a function and how the return value is retrieved.  Understanding this is crucial for interfacing between different parts of a program, especially when dealing with assembly language programming and understanding how the compiler and hardware interact.  Different architectures and compilers have varying conventions influencing performance and code compatibility.
syntax: The x86-64 calling convention typically uses registers for passing arguments. The first six integer arguments are passed in registers %rdi, %rsi, %rdx, %rcx, %r8, and %r9.  Floating-point arguments are passed in floating-point registers. The return value is typically stored in %rax (for integer values) or in %xmm0 (for floating-point values). The caller is responsible for saving and restoring any registers modified by the called function.
code_example:
section .data
y dq 3.14
x dd 10
z dq 1000
section .text
global _start
_start:
  movsd y, %xmm0 ; Load double argument y into xmm0
  movl x, %edi ; Load int argument x into rdi
  movq z, %rsi ; Load long argument z into rsi
  call f2 ; Call the function f2
  ; The return value (if any) will be in %xmm0
  ; ... rest of the program ...
example_explanation: This example demonstrates the x86-64 calling convention.  The arguments `y`, `x`, and `z` are passed to the function `f2` using registers %xmm0, %rdi, and %rsi respectively, matching the standard convention for double, int, and long arguments. The `call f2` instruction executes the function, and the result (if `f2` returns a floating point value) would be found in %xmm0. This exemplifies how hardware registers are used for passing data between functions at the machine level, a critical aspect of computer architecture and system programming.

extraction_metadata.source: Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective (3rd Edition)
